newsitem.title: USA: Starr confirms Vince Foster committed suicide.
newsitem.headline: Starr confirms Vince Foster committed suicide.

text.p: Whitewater prosecutor Kenneth Starr said on Tuesday evidence clearly showed former Deputy White House Counsel Vince Foster committed suicide four years ago and was not murdered.

Starr's report on the death that rocked the Clinton administration backed up the official version of what happened but was not likely to silence conspiracy theorists who claim Foster was killed on July 20, 1993.

"Based on investigation, analysis and review of the evidence by experts and experienced investigators and prosecutors, this office concluded that Mr. Foster committed suicide by gunshot," Starr said in a statement issued from his Washington office.

Authorities have consistently ruled out foul play in the case but Starr launched a fresh investigation after questions arose about whether documents had been removed from Foster's office on the night of his death.
Foster was a lifelong friend of President Bill Clinton and, like the president, was a native of the small Arkansas town of Hope.

He was also a partner and close ally of first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton at the Rose Law Firm in Little Rock when Clinton was Arkansas governor, and went to the White House when his friend became president in 1993.

Once there, Foster was assigned to handle the Clintons' personal financial and legal affairs, including their investment in the ill-fated Whitewater real estate project that lies at the centre of a web of business deals under investigation by Starr.

His death gave rise to a variety of bizarre conspiracy theories by opponents of the Clintons. Some of the theories even held that Clinton or his wife ordered their friend killed because he knew too much about their business and political dealings.
In Washington, a White House spokesman on Tuesday declined immediate comment on the Starr report.
Starr said his report was filed with the Special Division of U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit and would be made public at the court's discretion.
Foster's dead body was discovered on the evening of July 20, 1993, in a peaceful, suburban park just outside Washington.
He was found in his shirt-sleeves and his jacket lay nearby, folded neatly. Clutched in his hand was a decades-old revolver that authorities said belonged to his late father.
The U.S. Park Police, which led the initial investigation, concluded that Foster had placed the revolver inside his mouth and fired a single shot that killed him instantly.

Clinton was appearing on a national television interview when word of Foster's death reached the White House. When told what had happened, Clinton drove immediately to Foster's home to be with his friend's wife and children.
Foster was a mild-mannered man regarded as a skilled, methodical attorney and a perfectionist.
His widow, Lisa, returned to Little Rock after his death, and she last year married U.S. District Judge James Moody.
She was travelling on Tuesday and could not be reached. Moody declined to comment. Foster's family has consistently said it accepted the original finding that he committed suicide.
Starr's predecessor as Whitewater independent counsel, Robert Fiske, also concluded that Foster killed himself but Starr decided to take a fresh look at the case when he was chosen to replace Fiske.
Clinton's allies have accused Starr, a Republican, of leading a politically motivated campaign to discredit the Clintons. He denies the allegation.
